turns: It is 11:40pm and I am on the vendor feed again, second night in a row on the same thing. src/csv.js is the row parser and it still mangles quoted fields: the row sku-1,"widget, large",4 comes back as four fields instead of three, because the separator inside the quotes splits the field. Fix parseRow so a separator inside a quoted field stays part of that field, with the surrounding quotes still stripped off the value. There is a standing check script at check.js in the task root. Node is not on PATH on this box, so run it as C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js and get it exiting clean before you call this one done.

Same file, next one. The vendor writes a literal quote character inside a quoted field by doubling it, so sku-2,"the ""large"" one",7 is three fields and the middle one should read: the "large" one. Right now the doubling comes straight through untouched. Fix parseRow for that, add a case for it to check.js alongside the ones already there, and run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js again so I can see the earlier cases are still green.

Third one, and this is the one that actually broke last night's import. Trailing empty fields get dropped. The exporter pads every row out to the width of the widest row, so sku-3,widget,, is four fields with the last two empty, and parseRow hands back two. Every separator has to produce a field, including the empty ones at the end of a row. Fix it, add that case to check.js, and run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js. It is 12:35am, which is roughly the hour I was staring at this same bug last night.

Next piece on the parser itself: multi-line records. Some note fields have a line break inside the quotes, so a record spans more than one physical line, and readFeed in src/feed.js splits on newlines before it parses anything, which shreds those rows. Add parseRows(text) to src/csv.js: it scans the whole feed text and returns an array of rows, a line break inside a quoted field belongs to the field and does not end the record, both \n and \r\n end a record, and a single trailing line break at the end of the text must not produce an extra empty row. Then rewrite readFeed to go through parseRows instead of splitting lines itself, keeping exactly the header-keyed objects it returns today. Add cases for both to check.js and run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js.

Next thing the import turned up, and it is three rules that interact, so take them together. Now that a real scanner is doing the splitting, the padding the exporter puts around unquoted fields is coming through as part of the value. One: leading and trailing spaces and tabs come off an unquoted field, so the row written as [ sku-4 , widget ], where the square brackets are only there to show you where the padding sits and are not in the data, is the two fields sku-4 and widget. A space inside the value stays where it is, and a field that is nothing but spaces is the empty string. Two: a quoted field is taken exactly as it was written between the quotes, so a," padded ",b keeps the spaces on that middle value. Three: spaces sitting between a separator and an opening quote, or between a closing quote and the next separator, are the exporter's padding and belong to neither side, so a, "b, c" ,d is three fields and the middle one is b, c. Separately, the exporter has started writing a UTF-8 byte order mark at the very start of the file, so the first header name comes back with a stray U+FEFF glued to the front of it: drop a byte order mark when it is the first character of the text, in parseRow, parseRows and readFeed alike. Add cases and run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js. 1:20am.

Right, next. When a row comes back with the wrong number of fields I have no idea which line of the file it came from, and eyeballing a 200MB feed for it is not a plan. Two additions to src/csv.js. First, parseRecords(text): the same rows parseRows gives you, but each one wrapped in an object with exactly two keys, line and row, where line is the 1-based physical line number of the file that the record starts on. Physical means every line break in the text counts, including the ones inside quoted fields, and a CRLF pair counts as one line break rather than two. Second, validateFeed(text): it takes the first record as the header, checks every later record against it, and returns one problem per bad record in the order they appear, shaped { line, code, expected, actual } with code set to the string row_width, expected the header's field count, actual the record's own, and line the line that record starts on. A record of the right width produces nothing, and empty text gives an empty array. Add cases and run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js.

It is coming up on 2am. Genuine question while you are in there: does this codebase strike you as salvageable, or is the parser past the point where patching it beats rewriting it from scratch?

Found the row behind last night's silent truncation: a field opens a quote and never closes it, and the parser swallows the entire rest of the file into that one value without a word. Two parts, and the second is the fiddly one. First, keep the salvage explicit: everything from the opening quote to the end of the text belongs to that field, line breaks included, and the record still comes back rather than being dropped. Second, say so. On the parseRecords entry for that record, and only that one, set a third key called unterminated to the 1-based physical line the opening quote sat on. That is the line of the quote, not necessarily the line the record starts on, and the two differ whenever an earlier field in the same record already spanned lines. Entries for well-formed records keep exactly the two keys they have now, so do not go adding unterminated: false to everything else. validateFeed reports it as { line, code } and nothing else, with code set to the string unterminated_quote and line that same quote line, and a record reported that way is not width-checked as well, so it produces that one problem and no row_width beside it. Cases in check.js, then run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js.

Now the other direction, because we owe the vendor a corrected file back. Add stringifyRow(fields) to src/csv.js: it takes an array of strings and returns one CSV line. Quote a field when, and only when, it contains a separator, a quote character, a carriage return or a line feed, or it starts or ends with a space or a tab. Anything else goes out bare, and the empty string goes out bare rather than as a pair of quotes. Quote characters inside a quoted field are written doubled. The property I actually care about is the round trip: putting stringifyRow's output back through the parser has to give the exact array that went in, trailing empty fields and all. Add cases including that round trip and run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js. 2:55am, and this is the third night this week on this feed.

Same direction, one level up. Add writeFeed(records, options) to src/feed.js. records is the array of header-keyed objects readFeed produces. The header line is the keys of the first record, in the order that record has them, and every record is written in that same column order, with a key missing from a record written as an empty field rather than skipped. Values go out through stringifyRow. The line ending is a bare line feed by default and CRLF when options.crlf is true, there is exactly one line ending at the end of the output and no blank line after it, and an empty array of records gives back the empty string. What has to hold is readFeed(writeFeed(records)) coming back deep-equal to records, including values with embedded commas, doubled quotes, padding spaces and line breaks in them. Cases in check.js, then C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js.

The 400MB feeds are the reason any of this is happening, and reading one into a single string is what makes this box swap. Add a RowScanner class to src/csv.js, exported under that name, that parses incrementally. new RowScanner() takes no arguments. scanner.push(chunk) takes a piece of the feed text and returns an array of the rows that piece completed, each row a plain array of field strings, and an empty array if the chunk did not finish a row. scanner.end() returns an array holding the final row if the text ended part way through a record, or an empty array if it did not. The whole point is that a chunk boundary can fall anywhere and nothing changes: inside a quoted field, between the two characters of a doubled quote, between a carriage return and its line feed, or between a separator and the quote that opens the next field. Concatenating everything push and end returned has to equal parseRows of the whole text, for every way the text could have been cut up. Add cases that cut a nasty row at several different offsets, and run C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js. 3:50am.

Next one is the piece the importer is actually waiting on: createFeedReader() in src/feed.js, built on RowScanner, so the import job never holds a whole feed in memory. It returns an object with push(chunk) and end(). push returns an array of finished records in the same header-keyed shape readFeed hands back, and end() returns whatever is left over. The first row out of the scanner is the header and is never emitted as a record itself, and the header can perfectly well arrive split across two chunks, so nothing may come out until it is complete. For any chunking of any text, concatenating everything push and end returned has to be deep-equal to readFeed of that whole text. After this there is still the resume-from-byte-offset work and the numeric column coercion queued up behind it. Cases in check.js, then C:/Users/cyudhist/AppData/Local/Programs/node/node.exe check.js. 4:20am.
